cards.front: What counts as capability bloat in an agent's configuration?
cards.back: **Any tool, scope, credential or data field the agent holds that its role never uses.** Each one widens the blast radius of a mistake or an injection, and adds one more wrong choice for the model.

cards.front: A role's tasks never use a capability, even one kept because it might be useful someday. What does least privilege require?
cards.back: **Remove it: least privilege is subtraction.** Confirmation prompts, audit logs and time windows are compensating or detective controls for capabilities the role needs, never a substitute for removing one it does not (trap: T-REMOVE, Guard Instead of Remove).

cards.front: Why must tool allowlists be recertified on a schedule, and what test decides what gets pruned?
cards.back: **Because allowlists only grow.** Recertification prunes what no role still uses, and the test is whether any task in the role's job uses the capability, not how often it is called.

cards.front: Name three ways to narrow a capability that a role needs but that carries risk.
cards.back: **Caps, single-record scope and allowlisted targets.** Narrowing is for a capability the role genuinely uses, so removal is off the table: the action stays available while what one call can reach shrinks.

cards.front: A role needs a risky capability. What two factors set how it is gated, and where is that gate enforced?
cards.back: **Reversibility and blast radius set it, and the tool handler enforces it, not the prompt.** A limit written in the prompt only makes compliance more likely; a handler check holds on every call (trap: T-ENFORCE, Instruction as Guarantee).

cards.front: Wrong-tool picks rise as an agent's catalogue grows. Name the three moves that address the cause.
cards.back: **Scope toolsets per role, split along real domain seams and delete duplicates.** Mis-selection that rises with catalogue size is a bloat symptom, so the fix reduces and separates what each role sees rather than adding wording.

cards.front: Why does a mode-switch mega-tool fail to fix mis-selection in a large catalogue?
cards.back: **It only moves the confusion into a parameter.** The tool count drops, but the model must still choose among the same options through the mode argument. A routing paragraph fails too: it adds words, not separation (trap: T-MEGATOOL, Mega-tool Band-aid).

cards.front: When is sharpening tool descriptions the right first fix for wrong-tool picks, rather than role scoping?
cards.back: **When two tools overlap in a small, stable set.** That is a description problem, so sharpen those two descriptions first. Scoping, splitting and deleting duplicates are for confusion that grows with catalogue size.

cards.front: A tool is loaded, yet Claude never calls it. What does its description usually lack?
cards.back: **When to use it, and when not to.** A description that says only what the tool does gives the model no cue for choosing it. If calls stopped right after a host or config change, suspect that change first, not the unchanged description (trap: T-LAYER).

cards.front: In Claude Code, which tools does a subagent receive when its definition has no `tools` allowlist?
cards.back: **All of its parent's tools.** Omitting the allowlist hands the subagent the parent's full set of tools, so give each subagent its own `tools` list scoped to its job.

cards.front: Why must tool scoping be applied at every level of a Claude Code subagent tree, not just the top agent?
cards.back: **Current docs let subagents spawn subagents to a configurable depth**, and any level without a `tools` allowlist inherits everything its parent holds. Scoping only the top agent leaves every lower level with the full set.

cards.front: What does it mean to design tools around agent tasks rather than API endpoints?
cards.back: **Build a typed workflow tool for the task, not one tool per endpoint**: `schedule_event` finds availability and books, replacing a chain of `list_users`, `list_events` and `create_event` calls. Exception: if each step needs its own approval or audit entry, keep separate typed tools behind a workflow gate.

cards.front: What separates a sound `action` parameter from the mode-switch mega-tool trap?
cards.back: **One resource versus unrelated domains.** Related operations on one resource can share a tool with an `action` parameter; a `mode` switching between unrelated domains is the trap. Merging is no fix for overlap: two ambiguous descriptions just move that choice into the parameter (trap: T-MEGATOOL).

cards.front: When should an action be promoted out of a broad execute or shell tool into its own typed tool?
cards.back: **When it must be gated, audited or rendered.** Its own typed tool gives that action a handler where the gate, the audit entry or the rendering is applied, instead of leaving it one command among many inside the broad execute or shell tool.

cards.front: By which two parts should tool names be namespaced?
cards.back: **By service and resource**, as in `github_list_prs`: `github` is the service and `prs` the resource, with `list` as the action on it.

cards.front: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
cards.back: **Authentication proves who is calling; authorization decides what that caller may reach.** Most exam gaps are authorization at the wrong layer, not a missing login, so look for where the access decision is made.

cards.front: Name the two points where authorization should be enforced for an agent's data access.
cards.back: **Where the caller is first known, and again at the system that owns the data.** Both points sit outside the model, so the decision holds whatever the model is told or talked into.

cards.front: Why does a role check written into the system prompt fail as authorization?
cards.back: **It can be talked out of.** The model becomes the gatekeeper while the underlying access stays open, so one persuasive or injected request can get past it (trap: T-AUTHZ, Model as Gatekeeper).

cards.front: An agent reads data whose visibility differs by user. Whose permissions should it act with?
cards.back: **The calling user's own permissions, through a delegated, scoped identity.** A shared over-privileged service account erases the per-user boundary, and its audit trail names the integration, not the person who asked (trap: T-AUTHZ).

cards.front: Why does narrowing a shared service account to read-only still fail when each user may see different records?
cards.back: **One shared identity still reaches every user's records**, so the per-user boundary is gone however narrow its scope, and the audit trail names the integration. A scoped service identity fits only data that is non-sensitive and the same for every user (trap: T-AUTHZ).

cards.front: What is audience validation at an MCP server?
cards.back: **Accepting only tokens that were issued for that server.** A token issued for some other service is rejected even when it is genuine, so each service keeps its own authorization decision instead of trusting another's.

cards.front: An MCP server must call a downstream API for the user. Which token should it present?
cards.back: **Its own token for that downstream service, tied to the user.** Forwarding the caller's token is **token passthrough**, which the MCP spec forbids as a confused-deputy risk; swapping in a shared service credential ends passthrough but drops the per-user check (trap: T-AUTHZ).

cards.front: On a request to an MCP server, where must the token go, and where must it never go?
cards.back: **In the Authorization header, never in a query string.** It sits alongside the other MCP token rules: accept only tokens issued for this server, and never forward them downstream.

cards.front: Where should entitlement filtering happen in a retrieval-backed answer?
cards.back: **Inside the retrieval query, before data enters the context.** Redacting the answer acts after the exposure has already happened, because the restricted data was in the model's context first (trap: T-BOUNDARY, Control After Crossing).

cards.front: Which layer holds secrets, and which two places must they never appear?
cards.back: **The tool layer; never in prompts or committed config.** A secret in the prompt has already crossed into the model's context, and telling the model not to reveal it is no control (trap: T-BOUNDARY, Control After Crossing).

cards.front: A stem asks you to stop unauthorized access and prove who accessed what. Which two controls pair up?
cards.back: **Per-user authorization to prevent, plus an audit record keyed to the real user to detect.** Logging never replaces the preventive half (trap: T-DETECT, Detection for Prevention).

cards.front: In a shared multi-tenant index, where must the tenant filter come from?
cards.back: **The authenticated session, injected by the server**, never a tool argument the model fills in. Where contracts demand hard separation, also use per-tenant namespaces or indexes (trap: T-AUTHZ, Model as Gatekeeper).

cards.front: Why should the delay for entitlement changes to reach a search index be stated as a requirement?
cards.back: **Revocations above all must reach the index or its filter quickly.** Until a change propagates, a user who lost access can still retrieve the data, so the acceptable propagation delay is a requirement, not an accident.

cards.front: Name the three authorization rules for calls between internal agents.
cards.back: **Each agent has its own identity, the receiving agent enforces an allowlist of what each caller may ask for, and delegated scope never exceeds the original user's.** Internal agents need authorization between them too.

cards.front: An agent needs credentials to call services. What should inject them, and what two properties should they have?
cards.back: **The host or a vault, injecting them outside the model's context; short-lived where possible and rotatable without an outage.** Location comes first: rotating a key that still sits in the prompt leaves the new key just as exposed (trap: T-BOUNDARY).

cards.front: Why must a secret never be written into an agent's persistent memory?
cards.back: **Persistent memory replays it into later sessions.** The secret re-enters the context long after the task that needed it, instead of staying with the host or a vault outside the model.

cards.front: What is the first move in any latency decision, and which terms are the candidates?
cards.back: **Measure the dominant term**: time to first token, output length, sequential calls, retrieval and re-ranking spans, or peak queueing. Then pull the lever that targets it (trap: T-LEVER, Lever Before Measurement).

cards.front: A pipeline waits on the full model output before it acts. Would streaming shorten its latency?
cards.back: **No: the first tokens appear sooner, but completion time does not change.** Streaming helps a person watching the answer arrive, not a system waiting on the full result (trap: T-LEVER, Lever Before Measurement).

cards.front: Besides perceived speed, what reliability reason is there to stream a very long request?
cards.back: **Long requests without streaming can fail when networks drop idle connections.** Streaming keeps the connection alive, and the docs point very long outputs to streaming or Batch; it still does not meet a deadline on total completion time.

cards.front: How should a latency budget be stated?
cards.back: **As p95 at peak, with surge days included, never as an average.** The tail is where timeouts fire and users give up, so an average, or a budget that skips surge days, hides exactly when users suffer (trap: T-AVGSLA, SLA on Averages).

cards.front: What is tier routing?
cards.back: **Sending the measured easy slice to a faster tier and escalating the hard slice.** 'Measured' is the decider: the faster tier gets only the slice its evals show clears the floor, so capability is spent only where the hard slice needs it.

cards.front: How must the accuracy floor be verified after introducing tier routing?
cards.back: **Per slice at peak, not on the blended total.** A blended number can look healthy while the escalated or misrouted hard slice falls below the floor (trap: T-AGGREGATE, Average Hides Slice).

cards.front: When should you keep a single model tier instead of routing by difficulty?
cards.back: **When the slices overlap so often that misroutes cost more than the latency saved.** Routing pays only when easy and hard requests can be told apart well enough to send each to the right tier.

cards.front: What must justify adding a re-ranker or verification pass to a latency-budgeted pipeline?
cards.back: **The accuracy it buys on a named eval, weighed against the p95 it spends.** Every pipeline stage must earn its latency, so a stage whose accuracy gain has not been measured has not justified its place.

cards.front: Which lever targets each term: long output, a long stable prompt prefix, and independent calls?
cards.back: **Shorter templates and output caps for output length, caching for the long stable prefix, and parallel execution for independent calls.** Output length drives generation time; caching cuts input processing, not generation.

cards.front: Output is already capped and independent calls already run in parallel, yet a synchronous caller's hard timeout still expires. What pattern is left?
cards.back: **An async job with an ID.** The caller gets the job ID straight away and collects the result later, so the synchronous timeout no longer bounds the work.

cards.front: Name the three things a justified accuracy-latency configuration must state.
cards.back: **Measured accuracy per slice, p95 at peak, and the floor it respects.** Without all three, a configuration choice is an assertion rather than a justification.

cards.front: Why is a quality regression invisible to a team that captures only rate, errors and latency?
cards.back: **Those signals record nothing about content.** Instrumentation decides what gets recorded; dashboards, alerts and runbooks only consume it, so add content tracing before another dashboard (trap: T-OBSERVE, Fix Before Seeing).

cards.front: Name the contents of a usable trace for one request.
cards.back: **One correlation ID across every span, plus prompt and model versions, retrieved chunk IDs and scores, tool calls with arguments and results, per-span latency, token counts and the output.** Together they show which layer changed.

cards.front: How should a trace split token usage, and what must it record about stopping and human approval?
cards.back: **Token usage split into cache reads, cache writes, uncached input and output; the stop reason; and for any human approval, who approved, when, and what they saw.**

cards.front: Why do unbounded identifiers such as claim or user IDs stay out of metric labels, and where do they go?
cards.back: **Label cardinality is what makes metrics expensive, so they go in traces and logs.** Metrics keep bounded labels; unbounded identifiers such as claim or user IDs are recorded in traces and logs instead.

cards.front: Name four quality signals to record because infrastructure metrics miss them.
cards.back: **Refusals, escalations, overrides and guardrail blocks.** Quality failures look healthy to infrastructure metrics: a confident wrong answer and a refusal both arrive as successful responses.

cards.front: What is tail-based sampling?
cards.back: **Deciding which full payloads to keep once the outcome is known.** Every request gets a light correlated record; full payloads are kept for errors, escalations, overrides, flagged slices and a random baseline. Uniform sampling loses most rare failures.

cards.front: Why should a tail sampler hold payloads before deciding which to drop?
cards.back: **Late signals such as overrides arrive after the response.** Deciding too early discards exactly the runs a person later overrides, so payloads are held until those signals can arrive.

cards.front: An intermittent failure will not reproduce on demand. How should it be diagnosed?
cards.back: **From the captured original run, not by trying to reproduce it.** Keeping full payloads for failures means the evidence already exists when the investigation starts.

cards.front: How do you localise a quality regression from traces?
cards.back: **Compare failing and passing traces, sliced by what the change touched**: index version, prompt version, region or product. The slice where failures concentrate points to the layer that broke.

cards.front: Why can an aggregate quality metric stay flat through a real regression?
cards.back: **One slice can collapse while the rest hold the average steady.** Report and alert per slice, and gate on the worst critical slice rather than the blended number (trap: T-AGGREGATE, Average Hides Slice).

cards.front: Traces capture claim or health payloads. Which data rules do those traces inherit?
cards.back: **Residency, minimisation and retention rules**, the same as the data they contain, because traces are data too. Redact or tokenise sensitive fields at capture, and keep EU traces in the EU.

cards.front: A regime forbids storing content at all. What should traces still record?
cards.back: **Structure only: IDs, versions, token counts, scores and stop reasons.** Content quality is then evaluated on consented or synthetic sets rather than stored production payloads.

cards.front: What should decide chunk boundaries in a RAG pipeline?
cards.back: **The corpus's own units**: clause, section, endorsement, table or row. Chunks that follow the document's structure keep a rule and its exceptions in the same unit.

cards.front: What kind of defect does a fixed-size window create when it splits an exception from its rule?
cards.back: **A content defect** in the indexed text itself. No retrieval setting repairs it: raising top-k or swapping the embedding model does not reconnect text that ingestion cut apart, so fix the chunk boundary (trap: T-STUFF, Context Stuffing).

cards.front: Name the metadata a contextual header on a policy-wording chunk should carry.
cards.back: **Product, edition, jurisdiction, effective dates and section path.** Then a chunk saying 'this excess does not apply' still tells the reader which excess, where and when.

cards.front: What is Anthropic's contextual retrieval, and what did it achieve in published tests?
cards.back: **A short, generated context line prepended to each chunk before both embedding and BM25 indexing.** In Anthropic's published tests it cut failed retrievals by 49 percent, and by 67 percent with re-ranking.

cards.front: What is parent-document retrieval, and when is it used?
cards.back: **Index smaller child passages but return the whole parent unit.** Use it when a unit is too long to match well: the child gives precise matching, the parent gives complete context.

cards.front: Which index field type serves identifiers, which serves concepts, and which serves filters?
cards.back: **Lexical fields for identifiers and clause numbers, embeddings for concepts, structured fields for filters.** Index for the queries you expect: chunking decides what can be found, indexing decides how.

cards.front: One answer needs both policy wording and the claim's current status and reserves. Split by volatility, where does each part come from?
cards.back: **The wording from the index; status, reserves and payments from the system of record at request time**, composed with the retrieved text. The index holds slow-changing knowledge; faster re-indexing only serves stale state sooner (trap: T-LIVESTATE, Indexing Live State).

cards.front: When is chunk overlap a legitimate part of the fix for split units?
cards.back: **Only as a measured complement for units longer than a chunk**, alongside unit-boundary chunking or parent retrieval. Arbitrary overlap on its own cannot guarantee a unit stays whole.

cards.front: Answers degrade after a corpus refresh while model and prompt are unchanged. What do you suspect first?
cards.back: **Chunking, metadata and embeddings.** The refresh is the triggering change, so the ingestion layers it touched come before anything else (trap: T-LAYER, Blame Untouched Layer).

cards.front: Edits to scheduled documents lag in the index, and that lag is the measured cause. How is the index kept fresh?
cards.back: **Incremental upserts and deletes from change events, plus a periodic full rebuild to reconcile**, held against a stated maximum staleness. Re-indexing is right for documents that change on a schedule; only transactional state moves to a system-of-record call (trap: T-LIVESTATE).

cards.front: Before tuning retrieval, which two ingestion checks come first?
cards.back: **Count parse failures and check coverage against the source.** Nothing downstream recovers text that never arrived, so retrieval tuning cannot fix an ingestion gap.

cards.front: Name the three gates a refreshed index must pass before it goes live.
cards.back: **Complete, superseded versions purged, and one embedding model throughout.** The same rule means changing the embedding model requires re-embedding the whole corpus: never mix embedding spaces in one index.

cards.front: Before choosing lexical, semantic or hybrid retrieval, what must you classify first?
cards.back: **The traffic.** Exact identifiers (policy numbers, clause IDs, form codes) are a lexical problem, paraphrased concepts are semantic, and mixed traffic needs a hybrid retriever or a router.

cards.front: Why do exact identifiers such as policy numbers or clause IDs miss under embedding search?
cards.back: **Embeddings blur adjacent codes**, so a neighbouring identifier can come back instead of the one named. Identifiers are a lexical problem, and no bigger model fixes a retrieval miss (trap: T-BIGMODEL, Bigger Model Reflex).

cards.front: A question asks for a count, sum or range over structured records. How should it be answered?
cards.back: **Through a structured query in a tool**, not similarity search over rows turned into sentences. Top-k never adds up to an aggregate: it returns a handful of similar rows, never the full count or sum.

cards.front: Answers must come only from the jurisdiction and edition in force at the date of loss. What enforces that?
cards.back: **Metadata filters that narrow the search before or inside the query.** Headers showing the edition, plus an instruction to ignore out-of-scope passages, still leave the choice to the model: a prompt doing a filter's job (trap: T-ENFORCE, Instruction as Guarantee).

cards.front: Which retrieval defect does re-ranking fix, and what constraint does it carry?
cards.back: **A precision defect**: the right passage is in the candidate set but ranked too low, below noise. The re-ranker reorders those candidates, and its added latency must fit the p95 budget.

cards.front: When is widening k or adding sources the right retrieval fix?
cards.back: **Only for a measured recall gap**: the right passage never reaches the candidates, or every passage above the cut-off is relevant and the question needs more than k (one per compared item), so raise k to that count. Thrown at a precision problem, volume adds noise, cost and latency (trap: T-STUFF).

cards.front: How do you tell a retrieval defect from a grounding defect?
cards.back: **Wrong passages is a retrieval defect; right passages with a wrong answer is a grounding defect.** That is why retrieval is measured separately from generation, and per slice.

cards.front: A reference corpus is small, stable and fits comfortably in context with caching. What retrieval does it need?
cards.back: **Often none: load it whole in a cached prompt prefix, with no RAG**, since retrieval then only adds error. The line is well under ~200k tokens; once the corpus outgrows a comfortable fit, or recall and cost degrade, move it to an index.

cards.front: Name the query rewrites that can fix retrieval without changing the index.
cards.back: **Expand acronyms, pull out identifiers and split a multi-part question.** Query-side fixes often beat index changes; judge them on a sample of real production queries, not only curated ones.

cards.front: When should retrieval run as iterative multi-hop rather than a single query?
cards.back: **When the next query depends on the answer to the last one.** A single query cannot ask for what the system does not yet know, so each hop's result shapes the next search.

cards.front: When does soft recency boosting beat a hard effective-date filter?
cards.back: **When newer is better but older is not wrong.** A hard effective-date filter fits when an older version would be wrong, such as the edition in force at the date of loss.

cards.front: What rule picks the integration mechanism for a capability?
cards.back: **The lightest mechanism that reaches every consumer.** Reuse and reasoning decide it: who consumes the capability, and whether the other side reasons for itself (trap: T-PROTOCOL, Wrong Integration Mechanism).

cards.front: What decides between a direct API or CLI call and tools inside one app?
cards.back: **Whether a model chooses the action at runtime.** A direct API or CLI call suits one consumer or a fixed pipeline you own; tools inside one app suit a single model choosing among a few actions.

cards.front: When does an MCP server fit as the integration mechanism?
cards.back: **When several clients or teams need the same live capability at runtime.** Authentication, error handling and change management are then built once, not per integration. Sharing alone is not enough: know-how that fetches nothing is a Skill (trap: T-PROTOCOL).

cards.front: Name the three MCP primitives and who drives each.
cards.back: **Tools for actions the model chooses, resources for context the application supplies, prompts for templates a user invokes.** Map each capability to the primitive whose driver matches it.

cards.front: When is agent-to-agent the right integration mechanism?
cards.back: **Only when the counterpart reasons independently**, usually across an ownership boundary, and must negotiate rather than be called. If the other side just executes a function, an API or MCP fits instead (trap: T-PROTOCOL).

cards.front: What crosses the boundary in an agent-to-agent integration?
cards.back: **Only messages.** Each side keeps its own tools, data and credentials, so neither exposes its internal capabilities to the other side's reasoning, and each can refuse and fail independently.

cards.front: How does the A2A protocol relate to MCP?
cards.back: **It complements MCP.** A2A, now under the Linux Foundation, is the main open standard for agent-to-agent integration, while MCP connects a model to tools and data.

cards.front: Teams want to share procedures, templates and domain rules, with no external system involved. Which mechanism fits?
cards.back: **A Skill.** It packages know-how and connects to no external system; for know-how alone, an MCP server is overhead (trap: T-PROTOCOL, Wrong Integration Mechanism).

cards.front: Which authorization rules must an MCP server still follow once a capability moves behind it?
cards.back: **Validate audience, act with the caller's identity and never pass tokens through.** The integration mechanism never relaxes the auth rules (trap: T-AUTHZ, Model as Gatekeeper).

cards.front: Name the two conditions that make an MCP server right even for a single app.
cards.back: **The host accepts capabilities only over MCP, or the stem states reuse by other hosts.** A hoped-for future consumer is not stated reuse; without either condition, one consumer is better served by the lighter direct call (trap: T-PROTOCOL).

cards.front: What decides which deployment surface an enterprise should run Claude on?
cards.back: **Who operates inference and whose controls already govern it**: identity, billing, audit, residency and contract. Picking on features and bolting controls on later is the trap (trap: T-COMPLY, Legality on Scorecard).

cards.front: Who operates inference on Claude Platform on AWS, as opposed to Amazon Bedrock?
cards.back: **Anthropic operates Claude Platform on AWS and is the data processor**, with AWS providing sign-in and Marketplace billing. On Bedrock and Google Cloud, the cloud provider operates inference inside its own boundary.

cards.front: After choosing a deployment surface, what must you check and pin on it?
cards.back: **Check feature parity and pin model versions on that surface.** Model IDs, feature availability and retirement dates differ by surface (Claude API, Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry, Claude Platform on AWS).

cards.front: What is progressive discovery, as opposed to monolithic context?
cards.back: **Exposing a short index of names and one-line descriptions, and loading full definitions only when a request needs them.** Monolithic context loads every tool definition, instruction and reference up front.

cards.front: Name the two costs every always-loaded tool definition imposes.
cards.back: **Context on every request, and competition for attention during tool selection.** Both apply even when a call uses only one tool, which is why large catalogues move to on-demand loading.

cards.front: Name the three mechanisms that implement progressive discovery for tools and procedures.
cards.back: **Tool search over deferred tool definitions, Skills whose metadata stays in context while the body loads on trigger, and subagents that each hold a narrow toolset.**

cards.front: What is just-in-time loading for reference knowledge?
cards.back: **Keeping lightweight references in context** (file paths, stored queries, links) and reading documents through search or file tools when a task needs them. It is progressive discovery applied to knowledge.

cards.front: Why does tool search keep the prompt cache intact when editing the `tools` array does not?
cards.back: **Deferred definitions stay out of the cached prefix, and discovered ones are appended inline.** Editing the `tools` array itself changes the prefix and invalidates the whole cache.

cards.front: What does role scoping decide, and what does progressive discovery decide?
cards.back: **Scoping decides what a role may use; discovery decides when those definitions load.** Scope first, to what the role's tasks use rather than team lines, then defer the rest: a deferred tool the role should not hold is still in reach (trap: T-REMOVE, Guard Instead of Remove).

cards.front: Why is truncating every tool description so the whole catalogue fits the wrong fix?
cards.back: **It is a blunt cut that degrades selection on every tool.** Keep descriptions complete and load them on demand instead (trap: T-BLUNTCUT, Blunt Cut).

cards.front: When switching to progressive discovery, which tools should stay always loaded?
cards.back: **The most-used ones.** Discovery is a step that can fail, so the tools nearly every request needs should not wait on a search each time, while the long tail stays deferred behind discovery.

cards.front: After a switch to tool search, the agent says it has no tool for a job a deferred tool handles. What is the first move?
cards.back: **Read the discovery traces: compare what the agent searched for with that tool's name and description.** Discovery is a step that can fail, so find why it missed before pinning the tool or reverting to full loading, unless users are being harmed (trap: T-OBSERVE).

cards.front: Beyond the context it saves, which two metrics must you measure after switching to progressive discovery?
cards.back: **Selection accuracy and latency.** Discovery adds a step that can fail, so measure both after the switch rather than assuming that loading less context made selection better.

cards.front: When is loading the whole toolset up front the better choice than discovery?
cards.back: **When the toolset is small, stable and used by most requests.** Up-front loading is then fine: it caches as a stable prefix and has no discovery step to miss.
